blocks.text: Photography Educator: Tony Chirinos
©Tony Chirinos, Jaider, from the project Scarred

Photography Educator is a monthly series on Lenscratch that highlights outstanding photography teachers who inspire students of all ages. Each month, the series celebrates an educator’s insights, strategies, and excellence in fostering creativity and resilience.

For the month of November, I am honored to feature artist and educator Tony Chirinos whose work has shaped conversations around the fragility and strength of the human body and spirit. A fellow educator introduced me to Tony’s practice last year, and I had the pleasure of meeting him in person a few weeks ago at CENTER ’s Review Santa Fe. Tony also serves on CENTER’s board.

Deep curiosity and personal experience with death and impermanence guide his photography, resulting in images that are visually compelling and rich in meaning. With poetic grace, his work deepens my understanding of mortality and dying. As professor of photography at Miami Dade College for more than twenty years, Tony brings that same curiosity and commitment to his students, cultivating their creative growth and individual perspectives.

This article features a selection of Tony’s photographs from two projects Scarred and What the Land Remembers , reflections and photographs from some of his students, and an interview exploring his path as an educator and photographer. Together, these offer a window into the lasting impact of his artistic and educational practice.

In Tony’s words: Photography holds the power to convey deep emotion and tell compelling stories. My artistic vision is rooted in personal experience, guiding me to create documentary-style projects that explore ongoing narratives with themes of mortality and fragility. These elements serve as a silent undercurrent in my work, shaping my long-term projects with an enduring pulse, where each photograph contributes its own depth, range, and beauty to the broader story.

Inspired by pioneers in documentary photography and influenced by philosophical inquiries into perception and the human condition, my approach merges sculptural depth with immersive storytelling. Through my lens, I aim to challenge perceptions and invite contemplation, encouraging viewers to confront the vulnerability and resilience that define our shared humanity.

Driven by a desire to evoke emotion and provoke thought, my work seeks to forge a connection between creator and observer. I invite viewers to journey alongside me—to engage with images that resonate universally, revealing the profound impact of photography in shaping our understanding of life’s impermanence.

ES: Can you share a little about your path in photography? TC: My path in photography began in high school, when I realized I wanted to be an art photographer. I was fortunate to have a photography teacher, Susan Maguire, who encouraged me to take that desire seriously. That encouragement stayed with me throughout my life. My journey wasn’t a straight line. I studied photography at Miami Dade Community College and Florida International University before earning my MFA at Columbia University. Along the way, I developed a strong technical foundation, eventually working as a biomedical photographer and establishing the Medical Photography Department at Baptist Health Systems in 1989. That experience taught me to look closely, to be patient, and to understand the power of a photograph to reveal something we might otherwise overlook. But my deepest interest has always been in using photography to explore the human condition—our vulnerability, mortality, identity, and the things we carry with us through life. For more than four decades, I’ve photographed people, places, and traditions that speak to these concerns. Much of my work comes from my own experiences, my family history, and my ongoing search to understand where I come from and how memory shapes who we are. Teaching photography at Miami Dade College has also become an important part of my photographic journey. My students continually challenge me to look at photography differently and remind me why I fell in love with it in the first place. Receiving the Callanan Excellence in Teaching Award in 2019, which honors photography educators nominated by students or colleagues, affirms the work I continue doing in the classroom. Yet, at its core, what motivates me as both a teacher and an artist remains the same thing that drew me to photography as a young man: the desire to look more closely, to ask questions, and to make photographs that help me understand something about myself and the world around me.

ES: Did you have an influential photography mentor or teacher? What was their biggest impact on you as both an artist and a teacher? TC: Without a doubt, one of the most influential people in my life was Susan Maguire, my high school photography teacher. I was a young man who wanted to become an artist but didn’t really know what that meant or whether it was even possible. Susan introduced me to the work of great photographers through books and helped me understand that photography could be much more than making a beautiful picture. It could be a way of thinking, a way of telling stories, and a way of understanding the world. What I remember most, however, was her generosity and the faith she placed in me. When I finally managed to buy an enlarger but couldn’t afford a lens for it, she lent me one of hers every weekend. That might seem like a small gesture, but to me, it meant everything. She was helping me pursue something I could barely afford to dream about. Years later, when I published my first monograph, The Precipice, I dedicated the book to her. I wanted her to know that her encouragement had stayed with me all those years. I think Susan also shaped the kind of teacher I try to be today. I know what it feels like to be a young student with a passion but very little certainty about the future. I try to recognize that in my own students. Sometimes, what a student needs most is not another technical lesson but someone who believes in them and encourages them to keep going. I can teach students how to use a camera, understand light, and make stronger photographs. But I also hope to give them something Susan gave me: the confidence to believe that what they want to do with their lives is possible. I don’t think there is a greater gift a teacher can give a student.

ES: You have exhibited widely, published books and zines and won many prestigious awards in photography, including the Guggenheim Fellowship (congratulations), how do you share your experience and success as an artist with your students? TC: I think one of the most important things I can share with my students is that being an artist is not just about making photographs. It’s about commitment, curiosity, discipline, and being willing to pursue something even when the path isn’t always clear. I try to lead by example. I continue to make work, apply for grants, publish books, exhibit, and put myself in situations where I have to take risks and learn something new. I want my students to understand that you never stop being a student yourself. I also believe it’s important to show them that there are real opportunities to make a living in photography. That’s why I invite former students who are working in the field to speak to my classes. When my students meet people who once sat in the same classroom and are now working as photographers, artists, or creative professionals, they begin to see possibilities for themselves that they might not have considered. Although receiving the Guggenheim Fellowship was a pivotal moment in my career, I see that recognition as more than a personal accomplishment. It gives me an opportunity to encourage my students to take their own work seriously, believe in what they are doing, and understand that their voices matter. Ultimately, I want my students to leave my classroom with more than technical skills. I want them to develop the confidence to pursue their own ideas, the discipline to keep working, and the understanding that a meaningful life in photography is possible. If I can help even one student find the courage to follow that path, I feel I’ve done something worthwhile.

ES: What’s next for you as an artist? TC: I think what’s next for me is, in many ways, a continuation of what I’ve been doing throughout my life: following my curiosity and pursuing the questions that keep me up at night. I have several projects that I’m deeply committed to. One is What the Land Remembers , in which I’m documenting the transformation of Homestead, a place that has been part of my life for decades. I’m interested in what happens to our memories and our sense of belonging as the landscape around us changes. The project is personal, but I think it also speaks to something much larger about how we live and what we leave behind. I’m also working on Scarred , a project exploring the visible and invisible scars people carry. I’m photographing individuals and pairing their portraits with handwritten accounts of their experiences. I’m interested in the stories behind those scars, the things we carry with us, and the ways pain shapes who we become. I hope the project creates a space for empathy and reminds us that, despite our differences, we share more than we realize. I’m continuing to develop work that explores vulnerability, mortality, identity, and the human condition. These are subjects I keep returning to because I don’t think I’ve exhausted what they have to teach me. At this stage in my career, I also want to be more intentional about bringing my work into the world—seeking exhibition opportunities, placing my photographs in collections, continuing to publish (my next photobook will be published by L’Artiere), and connecting with people who might recognize something of their own experiences in my work. I’ve been making photographs for more than 40 years, and I still feel that I have so much to learn. I don’t know exactly where the work will take me, and I think that’s a good thing. If I knew all the answers before I started a project, there would be very little reason to make the photographs. For me, what’s next is to keep looking, keep asking questions, and remain open to the possibility that the next photograph might teach me something I didn’t know I was looking for.

ES: How do you help your students tap into curiosity and the creative process? TC: I actually don’t give my students traditional photography assignments where I tell them what to photograph. I believe they already have something incredibly valuable to work with: their own lives, their experiences, their families, their neighborhoods, and the things that interest or concern them. My job is to help them recognize the possibilities in what is already around them. I encourage them to be curious, to slow down, to look more carefully, and to ask themselves why something matters to them. Sometimes the most meaningful photographs come from subjects they’ve known their entire lives but have never really learned to see. Of course, I teach them the technical aspects of photography, visual literacy, and how to make decisions about light, composition, time, and perspective. We spend a great deal of time looking at photographs, discussing them, and participating in critiques. I want students to understand not only how to make a photograph, but also why they are making it. I think it’s important that students develop their own voices rather than simply learn to satisfy a teacher’s expectations. When they photograph something personal, something they genuinely care about, the work often becomes more honest and meaningful. They begin to discover things about themselves in the process. For me, teaching is less about giving students answers and more about helping them ask better questions. I want them to leave my classroom understanding that photography isn’t just about pointing a camera at something. It’s about learning to see, finding meaning in the world around them, and discovering what they have to say about it.

ES: What is the most meaningful part of your job? TC: The most meaningful part of my job is seeing my students grow into independent thinkers who have the confidence to find their own way, both as photographers and as individuals. I believe my responsibility as a teacher is to give students the tools they need to think for themselves, make their own decisions, and develop their own voices. At some point, the umbilical cord must be cut, and I believe that needs to happen sooner rather than later. My goal isn’t to create students who depend on me for answers. It’s to help them develop the confidence to ask their own questions, take risks, make mistakes, and learn from them. One of the greatest rewards is seeing former students build successful careers in photography and other creative fields. Carlos Goldman, who became the Director of Photography for Inter Miami CF, Arturo Alcala, who works as a fashion photographer, and Richard Ramos, an entrepreneur and co-owner of Cardinal Lab, are examples of former students who have gone on to establish themselves professionally in different ways. I’m proud of what they’ve accomplished, but what means the most to me is knowing that they have found their own paths. Their success reminds my current students that studying photography can lead to real opportunities, and that there isn’t just one way to build a meaningful career. Teaching has also taught me that I can’t measure my success by how much my students depend on me. I measure it by their ability to move forward without me. When a former student no longer needs my guidance, but still chooses to come back, share their experiences, or help the next generation, that’s incredibly rewarding. Ultimately, I hope my students leave my classroom with more than the ability to make good photographs. I want them to have the curiosity, discipline, and independence to navigate the world on their own terms. Watching them do that is probably the most meaningful part of being a teacher.

There is nothing more significant to a student than to have a mentor who inspires you to challenge the way you view and understand the world. For me, Tony Chirinos is that individual who not only supports me throughout my journey as a photographer, but constantly motivates me to achieve the highest caliber of work that I could produce. I have been lucky enough to have been under the tutelage of Tony for many years now, whose enthusiasm and high standards for art encourage me to continuously think critically of the world while feeding my ambition to create works of significance. Because of Tony, I came to view photography as a viable career path and was steered to pursue higher education, leading me to Pratt Institute where I was beyond equipped with the knowledge and technical skills needed to earn a BFA. Moreover, fueled by the strong community Tony has created and the vitality of his role as a professor, I plan to further my studies in hopes of becoming a professor myself. As I continue to learn and grow throughout my career, it is a true gift to know that I have a mentor that I can always rely on to help me navigate the complexities and challenges of being a photographer.
Brianna Acevedo

What to say about Tony Chirinos? He is certainly the most challenging professor I have ever had the pleasure of studying under. His passion is infectious, and always motivated me to do my best, not only in class, but in my personal life. He has an obvious passion for photography, yes, but his devotion to education is what sets him apart. His knowledge is an inspiration and a goal. The goal is not to photograph and think the way he does, the goal is to use the way we think to inspire our images and visual narratives. He adapts his teaching style to match each student’s preferred learning method, molding us to be the photographers we want to be. Although he does not sugarcoat things, his honesty is what has taught me the most about photography. He makes learning fun whilst always maintaining a deep respect for the craft. A master in his field, and still a humble and caring individual. Tony Chirinos is the model of what a true professor should be. I am a better photographer and a better person because I met him, and for that I am forever grateful.

I first met Tony back in Fall of 2022; I didn’t know what to expect. I still remember the first day I met him, he showed me around the darkroom and that was it, I got bit by the photography bug. It was the beginning of many days in that darkroom, a place that I genuinely consider my sanctuary. Being a part of the photographic program at Miami Dade College Kendall has helped me grow not only as a photographer but also as person, and I have no other than Tony Chirinos to thank for that. His passion, respect and work ethic for photography and its practice is something I admire and work hard at to implement in my life. I try to be a sponge and absorb as much of his knowledge of photography and its history as I possibly can. One of the many things I admire about Tony is that he truly and deeply cares about his students and wants us to grow. When I first began taking photo classes with him, I was (and to a certain extent still am) a very shy person, but Tony saw something in me that I had not seen in myself. When he asked me to be President of the Photo Club at MDC Kendall, I was hesitant at first to say yes but seeing that Tony believed in me and saw that I had the potential to lead, it shifted something inside me, something that I’ve carried with me ever since then. That decision changed the trajectory of my life. Tony has not only been my professor and mentor; he’s also been like a father to me. It’s an honor and privilege to know him.
Jadier Moreno IG: @jaider.m

Tony Chirinos is a Venezuelan-born documentary-style artist based in Miami. His career spans over forty years, exploring the theme of mortality and fragility. Chirinos is a recipient of fellowships including the prestigious John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation (2023), The Green Space Miami Grant (2024), Callanan Excellence in Teaching Award (2019), the South Florida Cultural Consortium (2010), and the William Talbott Hillman Foundation grant (2021) to financially assist in the printing production of his first monograph, “The Precipice.” Mr. Chirinos holds a Master of Fine Arts from Columbia University (2003). Trained as a Bio-medical photographer in 1985 at Miami Children’s Hospital, he went on to create the Medical Photography department at Baptist Health Systems in 1989. His work has been exhibited nationally and internationally, including participation in the III Bronx Latin American Art Biennial. His photographic series have been featured in Dear Dave, The British Journal of Photography, The Washington Post, Photo Eye, Edge of Humanity Magazine, Slate, Daily Mail, Business Insider, and Fotofilmic, among others. Chirinos was among 100 photographers who participated in Review Santa Fe in 2012, 2018, and 2019. His work is included in the collections of Museum of Fine Arts Houston, University of Colorado at Boulder, Candela Collection, Cuban Heritage Collection, Light Work, Photographic Center Northwest, Center for Creative Photography at the University of Arizona, and Mount Sinai Medical Center, among others. Mr. Chirinos is a professor of photography at Miami Dade College since 2003. Website: www.tonychirinos.com IG: @chirinostony
